title: Electrical Safety PPE: Complete Selection Guide with 4 Arc Flash Categories
text:
Electrical Safety & Standards

 Electrical Safety PPE: Complete Selection Guide

 Choosing the wrong PPE for an electrical task is as dangerous as wearing none at all. A Category 1 arc-rated shirt offers no protection for a task that requires Category 4 equipment.

 This guide covers every major type of electrical PPE, the standards that govern each item, and a clear selection tool to match PPE to your specific voltage and arc flash risk level.

 
 NFPA 70E Arc Categories 
 IEC 60900 Gloves 
 FR Clothing 
 PPE Inspection Checklist 
 




 Electrical PPE is not a single item. It is a layered system covering the hands, body, face, eyes, head, and feet -- each component rated to its own standard and matched to the specific hazard level of the work.


 Why PPE Selection Gets People Killed


 Most electrical injuries happen when PPE is present but wrong for the task.


 An engineer wears leather gloves instead of IEC 60900 insulating gloves. A technician puts on a cotton coverall instead of arc-rated fabric. A supervisor uses standard safety glasses instead of an arc-rated face shield.


 
 
 

 These substitutions feel safe. They are not. This guide removes the guesswork.


 
 
 2,000+

 Arc flash injuries per year in the US alone

 

 
 40 cal/cm²

 Maximum arc energy Category 4 PPE must withstand

 

 
 1.2 cal/cm²

 Energy level at which bare skin gets a second degree burn

 

 
 30 ms

 Time for a 30 mA RCD to trip -- your PPE must survive until then

 




 
 
 
 

 Advertisement 
 

 

 
 
 
 

 Advertisement 
 

 



 

 NFPA 70E Arc Flash PPE Categories: What Each Covers


 NFPA 70E classifies electrical PPE into four categories based on the minimum arc thermal performance value (ATPV) required in cal/cm².


 Higher category means higher energy hazard. You must match or exceed the required category -- going one level below is not acceptable.


 
 
 Cat 1

 Minimum 4 cal/cm²

 
 Arc rated long sleeve shirt or coverall

 Arc rated face shield or arc flash suit hood

 Arc rated safety glasses underneath

 Insulating gloves Class 00 minimum

 Hard hat, leather safety boots

 
 

 
 Cat 2

 Minimum 8 cal/cm²

 
 Arc rated clothing system: shirt plus pants

 Arc rated face shield rated 8 cal/cm² or hood

 Safety glasses underneath face shield

 Insulating gloves Class 0 minimum

 Hard hat, hearing protection, leather boots

 
 

 
 Cat 3

 Minimum 25 cal/cm²

 
 Arc rated suit over arc-rated clothing

 Arc rated balaclava under arc-rated hood

 Arc flash suit hood rated 25 cal/cm²

 Insulating gloves Class 1 minimum

 Hard hat under hood, hearing protection

 
 

 
 Cat 4

 Minimum 40 cal/cm²

 
 Heavy arc-rated suit with full coverage

 Arc flash suit hood rated 40 cal/cm²

 Arc rated balaclava, leather work gloves over insulating gloves

 Insulating gloves Class 2 minimum

 Leather safety boots rated to arc flash risk

 
 




 
 ⚠️ Critical Rule

 Never wear synthetic fabrics (polyester, nylon, rayon) under arc-rated clothing. Synthetics melt onto skin during an arc flash, causing far worse burns than the arc itself. Only 100% cotton or wool undergarments are acceptable under FR gear.




 Insulating Gloves: IEC 60900 Class Selection


 Insulating gloves are the most important single item of electrical PPE. They are the last line of defence between your hands and a live conductor.


 IEC 60900 defines six glove classes by maximum working voltage. Select the class that covers your system voltage with a comfortable margin -- never work at the upper limit of a class.


 
 
 Class 00

 500V AC

 750V DC

 

 
 Class 0

 1,000V AC

 1,500V DC

 

 
 Class 1

 7,500V AC

 11,250V DC

 

 
 Class 2

 17,000V AC

 25,500V DC

 

 
 Class 3

 26,500V AC

 39,750V DC

 

 
 Class 4

 36,000V AC

 54,000V DC

 




 
 Leather Protector Gloves

 Always wear leather protector gloves over insulating rubber gloves during live work. The leather protects the rubber from mechanical puncture, cuts, and abrasion. The rubber insulates. Both are always worn together -- never the leather alone.




 Complete Electrical PPE: Every Item and Its Standard


 
 
 🧤

 Insulating Gloves

 IEC 60900

 Rubber gloves rated by voltage class. Test by inflation before every use. Replace immediately if cracked, punctured, or beyond the 6 month retest date stamped on the cuff.

 

 
 🥽

 Arc Rated Face Shield

 ANSI Z87.1 / NFPA 70E

 Must be rated in cal/cm² equal to or exceeding the arc flash category. A standard polycarbonate face shield shatters in an arc event. Only arc-rated shields are acceptable.

 

 
 👕

 Arc Rated (FR) Clothing

 ASTM F1506

 Flame resistant fabric self extinguishes after when the ignition source is removed. The ATPV rating in cal/cm² must match or exceed the task category. Ordinary workwear is not FR.

 

 
 ⛑️

 Insulating Hard Hat

 IEC 60900 / ANSI Z89.1

 Class E electrical hard hats are rated to 20,000V. Class G is rated to 2,200V. Standard construction hard hats (Class C) offer no electrical protection whatsoever.

 

 
 🦺

 Insulating Safety Footwear

 EN ISO 20345

 EH rated (Electrical Hazard) boots provide resistance to live conductors at the sole. They must not be confused with anti static boots, which serve the opposite purpose.

 

 
 🦯

 Insulated Tools

 IEC 60900

 Individually rated to 1,000V AC. Look for the double triangle symbol and voltage rating on every handle. Multi piece composite handles can delaminate -- use factory insulated tools only.

 

 
 🧯

 Voltage Detector (Non Contact)

 IEC 61243-3

 Used to verify dead before touching any conductor. Test the detector on a known live source before and after every use to confirm it is working. A defective detector is worse than no detector.

 

 
 🛑

 Insulating Matting

 IEC 61111

 Placed under the operator's feet
